sections.heading: What does GORD feel like?
sections.body:
The NHS describes heartburn as a burning feeling in the middle of the chest, often with a sour taste, caused by stomach acid travelling up towards the throat. It is often worse after eating, when lying down and when bending over. If it keeps happening, it may be called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or GORD.

NHS inform lists other possible symptoms, including bloating, belching, vomiting, a hoarse voice and a sore throat. NIDDK, a United States institute, describes GERD (the American spelling) as a more severe and longer-lasting condition in which reflux of stomach contents into the oesophagus, the food pipe, causes repeated symptoms or complications.

The NHS says common triggers include coffee, tomatoes, alcohol, chocolate, and fatty or spicy foods. Smoking, being overweight, pregnancy, stress and some painkillers such as ibuprofen are also listed.

sections.heading: Is reflux different in babies and children?
sections.body:
NICE guidance on reflux in children and young people describes regurgitation, when a baby brings milk back up, as common and normal in infancy. The NHS says a baby with reflux does not usually need to see a doctor if they are happy, healthy and gaining weight, and that babies usually grow out of it by the age of 1. It suggests a GP visit if a baby is not improving after trying ways to ease reflux, or if reflux is still happening after the age of 1.

For formula-fed babies who often regurgitate and are very distressed, NICE sets out steps for clinicians. These include reviewing the feeding history, trying smaller, more frequent feeds, and then trying a thickened formula.

A children's hospital leaflet lists coughing, gagging, trouble swallowing and wheezing among the symptoms to raise with a GP or health visitor.

sections.heading: How is GORD diagnosed, and are tests needed?
sections.body:
NHS inform says a GP can often diagnose GORD from the symptoms and may start treatment without any tests. NIDDK likewise says doctors usually diagnose it from symptoms and medical history. Testing is generally kept for people whose symptoms do not improve with lifestyle changes and medicines, or where a complication or another condition is suspected.

The NHS says tests such as a gastroscopy may be used for severe or persistent cases. A gastroscopy is an examination in which a thin tube with a camera is passed down the throat to look at the lining of the food pipe and stomach.

NHS inform advises seeing a GP if symptoms happen several times a week, if over-the-counter medicines are not helping, or if there are signs of something more serious such as persistent vomiting, vomiting blood or unexplained weight loss. The NHS notes that severe chest pain can occur and may be mistaken for a heart attack, and says urgent medical help is needed rather than a routine appointment. In an emergency, call 999.

sections.heading: What treatments are used for GORD?
sections.body:
The NHS says pharmacies sell antacids, which neutralise stomach acid, and alginates, which form a coating that protects the oesophagus from acid. These ease symptoms but will not cure the problem, and should not be taken regularly for long periods.

If lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines do not help, a GP may prescribe a proton pump inhibitor. This is a medicine, such as omeprazole or lansoprazole, that reduces how much acid the stomach makes. The NHS says some people need to take it on a long-term basis. If it does not control symptoms, a medicine known as an H2 receptor antagonist may be recommended.

The NHS says surgery is rarely needed. NHS inform describes it as an option if medication does not control symptoms.

sections.heading: Living with reflux: what self-care helps?
sections.body:
The NHS lists several self-care measures. These include eating smaller, more frequent meals, avoiding trigger foods, and not eating within three to four hours of bed. It also suggests avoiding tight waistbands, not smoking, cutting back on alcohol and losing weight if needed. Raising the head of the bed may also help, but the NHS says extra pillows are not recommended.

NIDDK says that for people who are overweight or have obesity, a doctor may suggest losing weight. It lists foods and drinks commonly linked to symptoms, including citrus fruits, tomatoes, chocolate, mint, caffeine, alcohol, high-fat foods and spicy foods. It adds that people react differently, so a doctor may suggest cutting out particular foods to see what helps.

sections.heading: What problems can reflux cause?
sections.body:
NHS inform says long-term damage to the oesophagus from leaking stomach acid can lead to ulcers, scarring and changes to the cells of the oesophagus, which can increase the risk of oesophageal cancer. A hospital leaflet says narrowings of the oesophagus, called strictures, are most commonly caused by scarring from acid reflux and usually cause difficulty swallowing that develops gradually.

Barrett's oesophagus is a change in the lining at the lower end of the oesophagus, usually found through endoscopy. Hospital leaflets say long-term acid reflux is thought to be the main driver, and the changed cells are not cancerous but carry a small increased risk of becoming so. NICE guidance says a history of reflux symptoms and obesity are the main risk factors.

NHS inform says a hiatus hernia, where part of the stomach pushes up through the diaphragm, makes reflux more likely.

faqs.q: Is acid reflux the same as heartburn?
faqs.a: The NHS describes heartburn as the burning feeling in the chest from acid travelling up towards the throat. If it keeps happening, it may be called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or GORD. So heartburn is the symptom, and GORD is the longer-lasting condition behind it.

faqs.q: Do antacids cure GORD?
faqs.a: The NHS says antacids and alginates ease symptoms but will not cure the problem, and should not be taken regularly for long periods. A pharmacist can advise on them. If lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines are not helping, the NHS advises seeing a GP, who may prescribe a proton pump inhibitor, a medicine that reduces how much acid the stomach makes.

faqs.q: Is a camera test always needed for reflux?
faqs.a: No. NHS inform says a GP can often diagnose GORD from symptoms and may start treatment without tests. The NHS says tests such as a gastroscopy, where a thin tube with a camera is passed down the throat, may be used for severe or persistent cases.

faqs.q: Do babies grow out of reflux?
faqs.a: The NHS says babies usually grow out of reflux by the age of 1. It says a baby with reflux does not usually need to see a doctor if they are happy, healthy and gaining weight. It suggests a GP visit if the baby is not improving after trying ways to ease reflux, or if reflux is still happening after the age of 1.

faqs.q: When should someone see a doctor about heartburn?
faqs.a: The NHS advises seeing a GP if lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines are not helping, if heartburn happens most days, or if there are other symptoms such as food getting stuck in the throat, frequent sickness or weight loss for no reason. Severe chest pain needs urgent medical help rather than a routine appointment; in an emergency, call 999.

sections.heading: What does osteoarthritis feel like, and does it get worse?
sections.body:
Pain and stiffness in the affected joints are the main features of osteoarthritis. NHS sources say the symptoms may come and go in episodes, which can be related to activity levels and even the weather. Pain is often worse with activity, and stiffness is typically worst after rest or in the morning, easing once a person starts to move. Versus Arthritis says a short spell of stiffness after rest is common.

The knees, hips and small joints of the hands are the most common areas affected, and the big toes and feet can also be involved.

The NHS says the condition does not necessarily get any worse over time. Symptoms vary from person to person and between different joints, and in more severe cases they can be continuous. Some people have osteoarthritis without many symptoms at all.

sections.heading: How is osteoarthritis diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP or other healthcare professional asks about the symptoms and examines the joints. NHS inform says there is no single definitive test for osteoarthritis. A NICE draft evidence review says that, without features pointing to another problem, osteoarthritis can be diagnosed through history and examination alone.

NHS inform says an X-ray is not currently recommended for diagnosing osteoarthritis, although one can show how much joint damage there is. For the hip and knee, an X-ray is sometimes used to help the diagnosis. Versus Arthritis says doctors rarely use an X-ray or blood test for knee problems, mainly to rule out other causes. MedlinePlus notes that X-rays may show loss of joint space and bone spurs, and that some people who have these changes have no symptoms.

MedlinePlus says blood tests do not help diagnose osteoarthritis, but they can check for other conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or gout. NHS inform lists joint pain, tenderness, stiffness, swelling and restricted movement as reasons to contact a GP practice.

sections.heading: What treatments are used for osteoarthritis?
sections.body:
The NHS says osteoarthritis cannot be cured but that a number of treatments can relieve the symptoms. It groups the main options into lifestyle measures, pain medication and supportive therapies. NICE guidance calls therapeutic exercise and weight management core treatments, and NHS inform describes keeping the joint active and strengthening the muscles around it as the best way to manage symptoms.

For pain, the NHS describes creams containing an anti-inflammatory medicine (topical NSAIDs) as often used for the knees and hands, and NICE advises offering one for knee osteoarthritis. Capsaicin cream is another option, and burning is its most common side effect. The NHS describes paracetamol as suitable for short-term use. NSAID tablets are generally considered if creams do not help, and because they can wear down the stomach lining, a medicine that reduces stomach acid may be given alongside them. Opioids such as codeine are generally limited to short-term use because of their side effects.

Steroid injections are sometimes offered when other treatments have not worked, and the NHS says they can ease pain for several weeks or months. NICE says to consider a corticosteroid injection into the joint when other medicines are ineffective or unsuitable.

sections.heading: What can help with osteoarthritis day to day?
sections.body:
The NHS says supportive aids such as shock-absorbing footwear, insoles, braces and walking sticks can reduce strain on the joints during everyday activities. Patient leaflets from NHS services describe pacing, which means balancing rest and activity, and note that taking on too much on a low-pain day can lead to worse pain afterwards. Supportive shoes are described as improving comfort and balance, and a walking stick can take pressure off an affected hip.

The leaflets describe heat as often suggested for stiffness or aching and cold for a sudden flare-up or swelling, with packs wrapped in a cloth. A physiotherapist can help build a plan guided by a person's symptoms, physical function and goals.

The NHS says GPs no longer prescribe glucosamine and chondroitin supplements on the NHS, because there is no strong evidence that they work.

sections.heading: When is surgery considered?
sections.body:
NHS inform says surgery is reserved for cases where other treatments have not been effective or where a joint is severely affected. It may greatly improve symptoms, but it cannot be guaranteed to resolve them fully. Versus Arthritis describes lifestyle changes, medication, therapies and, rarely, surgery as the ways to help.

MedlinePlus says non-surgical treatments often delay surgery or keep symptoms mild enough that it is not needed. The operations it lists include trimming damaged cartilage through a keyhole procedure (arthroscopy), realigning bone (osteotomy), fusing a joint, and partial or total joint replacement. NHS inform says joint replacement is the most common surgical option and that the decision is made with an orthopaedic surgeon, a doctor who specialises in bone and joint surgery.

faqs.q: Can osteoarthritis be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no cure for osteoarthritis, but treatments can relieve the symptoms. It groups the main options into lifestyle measures, pain medication and supportive therapies. The NHS also says the condition does not necessarily get any worse over time, and symptoms vary from person to person. NICE guidance describes therapeutic exercise and weight management as core treatments.

faqs.q: Is an X-ray needed to diagnose osteoarthritis?
faqs.a: NHS inform says an X-ray is not currently recommended for diagnosing osteoarthritis, although one can show how much joint damage is present. A GP asks about the symptoms and examines the joints, and there is no single definitive test. MedlinePlus notes that some people who have X-ray changes have no symptoms. Blood tests are used to look for other conditions, not to confirm osteoarthritis.

faqs.q: Do osteoarthritis symptoms come and go?
faqs.a: NHS sources say the symptoms may come and go in episodes, which can be related to activity levels and even the weather. Pain is often worse with activity, and stiffness is typically worst after rest or in the morning, easing with movement. Severity varies between people and between joints, and some people have osteoarthritis without many symptoms.

faqs.q: Do glucosamine and chondroitin supplements help?
faqs.a: The NHS says GPs no longer prescribe glucosamine and chondroitin on the NHS, because there is no strong evidence that they work. The options the NHS does describe are lifestyle measures, pain medication such as creams, and supportive therapies and aids such as footwear, insoles, braces and walking sticks.

faqs.q: Does everyone with osteoarthritis need surgery?
faqs.a: No. NHS inform says surgery is reserved for cases where other treatments have not been effective or where a joint is severely affected. MedlinePlus says non-surgical treatments often delay surgery or keep symptoms mild enough that it is not needed. When surgery is considered, the options include fusing a joint and partial or total joint replacement, decided with an orthopaedic surgeon.

sections.heading: What does a UTI feel like?
sections.body:
NHS guidance lists pain or a burning feeling when passing urine, needing to go more often than usual, cloudy urine, blood in the urine, and pain in the lower tummy or in the back just under the ribs. Feeling tired or weak and smelly urine can also occur. NIDDK, a US health institute, describes similar bladder infection symptoms, including discomfort in the lower abdomen and cloudy, bloody or strong-smelling urine.

When a bladder infection spreads to one or both kidneys, NIDDK lists fever and chills, nausea or vomiting, and pain in the back, side or groin as warning signs. It says early treatment prevents most complications. MedlinePlus says bladder infection symptoms usually improve within a day or two of starting treatment, while kidney infections can take a week or more to resolve.

sections.heading: How does a UTI show up in older people and children?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus says older adults may show only confusion. The NHS says that in older, frail people with memory problems such as dementia, and in people with a urinary catheter, symptoms can include changes in behaviour such as acting agitated or confused, wetting that is worse than usual, or new shivering or shaking.

In babies and young children, fever is the most common sign and may be the only one. Poor feeding and vomiting can also occur. Children who were toilet trained may start having accidents by day or night. MedlinePlus says antibiotics for a child's UTI should start quickly to protect the kidneys, and a child under six months old, or with other complications, should see a specialist right away.

sections.heading: How is a UTI diagnosed?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus describes urinary tract infections as affecting the bladder, kidneys, ureters or urethra, and calls a kidney infection pyelonephritis. A urine culture identifies the bacteria so a clinician can choose an antibiotic. A positive culture, meaning bacteria or yeast grew, likely indicates a UTI, although earlier antibiotic use can produce a falsely negative result.

For older adults, the NICE quality standard recommends diagnosing UTI by full clinical assessment, without a urine dipstick test, because dipstick accuracy varies. A UK hospital study of older patients found that most positive dipstick results did not match the laboratory result. The NHS England and UKHSA toolkit likewise says dipsticks should be avoided in older adults to support an accurate diagnosis.

sections.heading: What treatments are used?
sections.body:
NIDDK says a health professional will likely prescribe antibiotics for a bacterial bladder infection, and the length of treatment depends on how severe the infection is and whether symptoms go away. It advises finishing the whole course, because antibiotic resistance could make an infection harder to treat, and says drinking more liquids, with water best, can speed recovery and ease symptoms.

The NHS says antibiotics are not always needed. A GP may offer self-care advice and a painkiller, a short course of antibiotics, or a prescription to use after waiting 48 hours in case symptoms go away alone.

For kidney infection, the NHS says most people are treated at home with antibiotics. Paracetamol helps with pain and high temperature, and ibuprofen-type painkillers are not normally recommended because they may increase the risk of further kidney problems. Hospital treatment with antibiotics through a drip may be needed for people who are pregnant, have a long-term health condition, are severely dehydrated or cannot keep down fluids or medicines.

sections.heading: Why do some people get UTIs again and again?
sections.body:
Reviews define recurrent UTI as two infections within six months or three within twelve months. NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP if a UTI returns after treatment or follows that pattern. Options it lists include a different antibiotic, a low-dose antibiotic taken for up to six months, or, after the menopause, an oestrogen vaginal product. NHS patient information also describes taking antibiotics after sex where sex seems to trigger infections.

NIDDK says vaginal oestrogen increases good bacteria and helps prevent infection, and that diaphragms, unlubricated condoms or spermicide may raise the chance of a bladder infection. It says cranberry products do not treat an existing infection and there is not enough evidence to be sure they prevent one.

sections.heading: Can a UTI become serious, and who should be contacted?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus lists kidney infection and sepsis, a dangerous overreaction to infection, as risks of a UTI, with sepsis risk greatest in young children, very old adults and people with weakened immunity. NHS England says older adults made up almost three fifths of UTI hospital admissions over five years.

NHS 111 Wales advises calling 999 or going to A&E if a person with a suspected UTI, or their child, is confused, drowsy or has difficulty speaking, and not driving themselves. NHS guidance advises urgent help from a GP or NHS 111 for a very high or very low temperature, vomiting, blood in the urine, passing no urine all day, or symptoms that get worse quickly or do not improve within 48 hours. NI Direct says to see a GP if symptoms are very uncomfortable or last more than five days.

faqs.q: Can a UTI get better without antibiotics?
faqs.a: NHS 111 Wales says antibiotics may treat UTIs but are not always needed. A GP may offer self-care advice and a painkiller, a short course of antibiotics, or a prescription to use after waiting 48 hours in case symptoms go away alone. NHS guidance says symptoms that do not improve within 48 hours need review by a GP or NHS 111.

faqs.q: How is a kidney infection different from a bladder infection?
faqs.a: NIDDK says a bladder infection can spread to one or both kidneys, with warning signs of fever and chills, nausea or vomiting, and pain in the back, side or groin. MedlinePlus says kidney infections can take a week or more to resolve. The NHS describes blood poisoning as a medical emergency.

faqs.q: What are the signs of a UTI in babies and children?
faqs.a: Fever is the most common sign in children under one and may be the only one, with poor feeding and vomiting also possible. Children who were toilet trained may start having accidents by day or night. MedlinePlus says a child under six months old, or with other complications, should see a specialist right away.

faqs.q: When should someone see a GP about a UTI?
faqs.a: NI Direct says to see a GP if symptoms are very uncomfortable or last more than five days, or if there is a high temperature, symptoms suddenly worsen, or the person is pregnant or has diabetes. NHS 111 Wales advises calling 999 or going to A&E for confusion, drowsiness or difficulty speaking.

sections.heading: What does rheumatoid arthritis feel like?
sections.body:
The NHS describes rheumatoid arthritis (RA) as a long-term condition that causes pain, swelling and stiffness in the joints. It commonly involves the hands, wrists and feet, and the small joints of the hands and feet are often affected first. Joint pain, swelling and stiffness are the core symptoms. Stiffness is often worse in the morning or after rest, and it usually lasts longer than the stiffness seen in osteoarthritis.

Inflamed joints can swell and feel warm and tender, and firm lumps called rheumatoid nodules sometimes form under the skin. Symptoms most often begin slowly over weeks to a few months. Some people also have general symptoms, including tiredness, fever, sweating, poor appetite and weight loss. Inflammation can also affect the eyes, causing dryness, or the heart and lungs, causing chest pain. Symptoms vary between people and can come and go.

sections.heading: What is a flare-up and what can help?
sections.body:
Symptoms can come back or get worse, which is known as a flare-up. One NHS trust lists stopping or winding down treatment, doing too much, stress, infection and poor sleep as causes of flares.

Guidance broadly describes heat as easing stiffness and cold as easing swelling, and sources stress placing a towel between the skin and the heat or cold source. Sources recommend gentle movement rather than rest alone. NRAS, a rheumatoid arthritis charity, says exercise is important because it helps reduce the risk of further joint damage. NRAS advises speaking to the rheumatology team about regular flares, or a flare that is not going down with self-management. A Worcestershire hospital trust adds that recurrent flares can show that a change to treatment is needed.

sections.heading: How is rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed?
sections.body:
Rheumatoid arthritis can be difficult to diagnose because many conditions cause joint stiffness and inflammation, and there is no definitive test for it. The NHS advises seeing a GP if these symptoms appear. The GP carries out a physical examination, checking the joints for swelling and how easily they move. If the GP thinks the person has rheumatoid arthritis, they refer them to a specialist called a rheumatologist.

Blood tests include ESR and CRP for inflammation, a full blood count, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP. People who test positive for anti-CCP are very likely to develop rheumatoid arthritis, but not everybody with the condition has this antibody. A Manchester guide for GPs notes that a negative result does not exclude the condition and a positive result does not equate to a diagnosis. X-rays and MRI scans may be used to check for joint inflammation and damage, and ultrasound is used in some early arthritis clinics. Seropositive means these antibodies are found in the blood, and seronegative means they are not.

sections.heading: What medicines are used to treat it?
sections.body:
The NHS says treatments can help reduce inflammation in the joints, relieve pain, prevent or slow down joint damage, reduce disability and enable people to be as active as possible. Care usually involves the GP and several specialists. The disease-modifying medicines fall into two main groups, disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) and biological treatments.

Initial treatment is usually a combination of DMARD tablets, and methotrexate is usually the first medicine given. Biological treatments are generally used alongside methotrexate or another DMARD, typically when DMARDs alone have not worked. JAK inhibitors are offered to adults with moderate to severe disease who cannot take DMARDs or biological treatments, or who found them ineffective. Steroids can be given as tablets or injections and are usually used for short periods. The NHS says long-term steroid use can have serious side effects.

sections.heading: Monitoring and supportive care
sections.body:
The NHS says methotrexate can affect blood cells and the liver, so regular blood tests are used to monitor this. MedlinePlus says DMARDs may have serious side effects, so frequent blood tests and other monitoring are needed. MedlinePlus also says corticosteroids work very well to reduce joint swelling and inflammation, but they can have long-term side effects and do not prevent joint damage if used alone.

NHS inform lists physiotherapy, which helps improve muscle strength, flexibility and fitness. If the condition causes problems with everyday tasks, occupational therapy may help, and an occupational therapist can provide training and advice to protect the joints at home and at work. A support for the joints, such as a splint, may also be recommended.

sections.heading: Surgery and outlook
sections.body:
The NHS says surgery may be needed to improve joint movement, reduce pain or correct joint damage, and some people need a hip, knee or shoulder joint replaced. NHS inform lists hand and wrist surgery and arthroscopy among the options. The NHS notes that some function may not be restored after a damaged joint is replaced by a prosthetic one.

NHS inform says there is no cure for rheumatoid arthritis, but with treatment symptoms such as joint pain, swelling and stiffness improve. Other NHS sites agree that early treatment reduces the risk of joint damage. One review says rheumatoid nodules in the lung are usually symptom-free and often resolve on their own. One source says clinical remission is reached and sustained in a minority of people, and that drug-free remission remains rare.

faqs.q: Can rheumatoid arthritis be cured?
faqs.a: NHS inform says there is no cure for rheumatoid arthritis, but with treatment symptoms such as joint pain, swelling and stiffness improve. The NHS says treatments can help reduce inflammation, relieve pain, prevent or slow down joint damage and reduce disability. One source says clinical remission is reached and sustained in a minority of people, and drug-free remission remains rare.

faqs.q: What does seropositive rheumatoid arthritis mean?
faqs.a: Seropositive means rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP antibodies are found in the blood, and seronegative means they are not. People who test positive for anti-CCP are very likely to develop rheumatoid arthritis, but not everybody with the condition has this antibody.

faqs.q: Why are regular blood tests needed during treatment?
faqs.a: The NHS says methotrexate can affect blood cells and the liver, so regular blood tests monitor this. MedlinePlus says DMARDs may have serious side effects, so frequent blood tests and other monitoring are needed. One NHS trust leaflet says hydroxychloroquine does not need blood monitoring checks, although people taking it still have regular checks for other reasons.

faqs.q: Does rheumatoid arthritis only affect the joints?
faqs.a: Joints are the main target, but the NHS lists general symptoms that can occur, including tiredness, fever, sweating, poor appetite and weight loss. It says inflammation can also affect the eyes, causing dryness, or the heart and lungs, causing chest pain.

faqs.q: Does everyone with rheumatoid arthritis need surgery?
faqs.a: The NHS says surgery may be needed to improve joint movement, reduce pain or correct joint damage, and some people need a hip, knee or shoulder joint replaced. NHS inform describes surgery as sometimes needed, alongside medicines, physiotherapy and occupational therapy, so it is not described as needed by everyone.

faqs.q: What can trigger a flare?
faqs.a: One NHS trust lists stopping or winding down treatment, doing too much, stress, infection and poor sleep. Another source notes that a flare is often the result of several factors building up together. NRAS advises speaking to the rheumatology team about regular flares, or a flare that is not going down with self-management.
